title: Why no figures in mosques
hookLine: mosques avoid images of living beings, so pattern and word fill the walls

cards: A small child, maybe on a first visit to a big mosque, tugs a parent's sleeve and whispers: where are the pictures? It's a fair question. The walls are covered, floor to ceiling.
Tiles in blue and white. Stars inside stars. Vines curling into vines.
Lines of Arabic running around the dome. But no faces. No saints, no prophets, no animals, no people at all.
Every inch decorated, and not one living creature in sight. Today: image-makers.

teach.b: Start with God. The Qur'an says of Him: "Naught is as His likeness." Muslims take that to mean nothing in creation can picture God, so a mosque never tries.
Then the prophets: Muslims honor them, and a mosque doesn't paint them on its walls to be gazed at in prayer. Then the hadith.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns sternly against image-makers, who on the Day of Judgment are told to breathe life into what they made, and cannot.
Another report says angels don't enter a house where there are pictures. And there's a very human story, also in Bukhari.
A man who made his living painting pictures came to Ibn Abbas, a companion of the Prophet, worried about his work.
Ibn Abbas told him the warning, then gave him a way through: if you must paint, paint trees, and things that have no soul.

Scholars read these reports in different ways. Some hold that every image of a living being is forbidden. Others say the concern is statues, or images that could be worshiped, and allow pictures in books or homes.

And some Muslim lands, such as Persia and Mughal India, have rich traditions of painted figures in manuscripts and palaces. But the mosque, the place of prayer, keeps the figures out. So what fills the walls?
The word, as in calligraphy. And pattern: stars, vines, interlacing lines that never settle on one creature to look at. The eye keeps moving, past the tile, past the wall.

how: Mosques are decorated with calligraphy, geometric patterns and plant designs rather than images of people or animals; Muslim scholars differ on pictures outside the mosque, and some Muslim lands have long traditions of painted manuscripts.

games.q: you make your living painting pictures, and you've just heard the warning to image-makers. you go to Ibn Abbas, worried. what does he tell you?
o: if you must paint, paint trees and things without a soul.
games.why: he tells the painter the warning, then offers a way through: paint trees, and things that have no soul.

practice: Let your eyes move slowly around wherever you are, a tiled floor, the weave of a sweater, bricks, leaves outside, until you find one pattern to stay with.
Follow it to its edge, and notice how your eye wants to keep going, as though it carries on somewhere you can't see. If you pray, let that pull point you toward God; if not, just follow the line.

wordCard.voice: Image-makers, warned against in a hadith that says they'll be told, on Judgment Day, to breathe life into what they made, and cannot, which is why pattern and word fill a mosque's walls instead. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a form, an image or picture, the word at the heart of the debate.

carryVoice: Your line: pattern points past itself. A wall with no faces can still lead the eye somewhere. Same time tomorrow.
